posts.text:
Last wk, earnings had elements of all the AI issues I feared in my preview. $GOOGL – AI disintermediation fear for search and big FCF miss. $MSFT – neocloud partner pushing out capacity and 1st new fundraising bonds since 2017. $AMZN – AI growth miss in AWS and FCF miss.

Tech took a beating last week with Nasdaq -2.0% and Mag7 -2.4% but with S&P down only 0.6%. However, the nine non-tech related sub sectors (out of the eleven total) were strong and up 1.0-3.1%. As a result, the equal weighted S&P was up 0.8%. The above three names all declined last week with Google down 12.6%, Amazon -3.1% and Microsoft -0.5%. The historic 28.6% stock decline by $INTC on Friday (-24.4% for the week) did not help. This helped drive the SOX Index down 7.2% on Friday though the weekly decline was only 0.8%.

With all the hyperscalers now having reported, here are my current thoughts:

1) Microsoft has committed to staying FCF positive (with $18.6B in FCF in CQ3) and is the only name in this list that has committed to do so. M365 is likely to become the default option for enterprises that want AI in a safe environment through use of Co-Pilot.

2) Meta is using AI to improve the efficiency of their business as seen in their ad revenues compared to Google. Also Muse has been a hit with consumers for Agentic AI while they are appealing to enterprises with their strong open-weight models. An 18x CY27 PE for 28% revenue growth is appealing. Their major blemish is the future negative FCF expected with a $2.1B burn in Q3 driving them to raise ~$95B in equity financing following earnings results. S&P Global Ratings on cash flow concerns and AI spending revised their credit rating today from AA- stable to AA- negative.

3) Amazon despite missing buyside AWS expectations of ~42% y/y growth with 39% reported (official sellside consensus of 38%) expects 40% revenue growth for AWS in CY27 and CY28 despite being the largest public cloud vendor. Also their LTM FCF burn of $42.4B in Q3 vs $7.6B in June helped lead to a $80B supplier financing arrangement facility post-earnings. Also physical AI should benefit their e-commerce business. Both e-commerce and AWS were guided to be $1 trillion revenue businesses within the next 5-10 years.

4) Google’s new LLM model is back at the frontier with a low cost per token. However this miss in search revenues for the 2nd quarter in a row and first miss in both total revenues and EPS for the first time since late 2022 raises AI disintermediation fears. FCF burn of $9.1B was also more than expectations. But total search queries are at the highest levels in five years. As a result, as ad coverage and loads increase on their AI queries, these fears should pass much like in late 2025. Ultimately, I believe Google will be a winner in consumer AI through their distribution through Android phones.

As for Intel, I did not see this coming. On October 20th, $SMCI (purely enterprise related revenues) pre-announced 27% revenue upside along with a raise to gross margins guidance to 12-12.5% from 10.4%-10.8% for their CQ3. I am not a fan of SuperMicro to be clear. For the processor vendors, I thought upside in server revenues due to Agentic AI would offset the downside in their PC business due to memory related price increases lowering demand. $AMD, which is gaining share, reports earnings on Tuesday. This will help investors understand whether this is an Intel specific issue or industry issue. I would note that Microsoft’s guidance for their Windows OEM & Devices business was down ~35% y/y for December vs -22% in September and -7% in June.

Longer-term, I believe Intel will become a force in the foundry industry but in the near-term it may take some time for the valuation to reset lower due to their current microprocessor business.

posts.name: Matthew Chang
posts.text:
America is building so fast, we’re out of capacity.  It’s a CAPEX hurricane.  And it’s just beginning.

Four things before we get started:
1) Lock up your steel now
2) Secure your engineering team 
3) Project manage your long lead equipment
4) Make a friend in trucking, ASAP

You’ve heard President Trump say the industrial investment is measured in the trillions. At the same, I’ve seen accounts on this app claim industrial spending is decreasing because they are reading some market for Fed report.  Not true.

On The ReForge Podcast, you’ve heard me and Colin say all year that manufacturing and heavy industry are exploding. Several billion $ in new announcements come out every week. 

But instead of headlines or Fed reports, let me teach you a Floridian trick.  If you want to know if you’re in a hurricane, go stand outside.  If you’re in a hurricane, you can feel the air pressure in your bones, you can smell it (yes they have a smell), you will get wet was water droplets pelt your face, and you’ll feel the wind - fast and turbulent.  Then you can look at the trees.  You won’t see any birds or insects.  And if part of some guys roof blows by you, run inside and take shelter. YOU ARE IN A HURRICANE.  And you didn’t need to read an article or study data to know that you are. 

Now, we try to bring folks along and share data and stories.  But Colin and I grew up in manufacturing. I’ve done it exclusively for 21 years. 11 years of design-build construction and 10 years of industrial robotics.  I’ve filed 100+ state and local permits. I’m licensed as an engineer and general contractor.  I manage complex supply chains and take prime contracts.  My company offers performance guarantees, liquidated damages, bonding, and about 15 insurances. All that to say, I’m in the industry, I am from the industry.  I am the Florida man of manufacturing CAPEX.

I’m standing outside and I can feel it in my bones, on my skin, and the turbulence is starting to break all normal systems. 

We are in an industrial CAPEX hurricane. A face melting, mind bending, industrial CAPEX hurricane.

And it’s not going to stop anytime soon.  It’s a big and wide CAT 5, and news reporters will soon demand a new category for CAT 6.  That’s how big this storm is.

So what to do?  Take shelter.  It’s too late to board up the windows. It’s too big to make sand bags.  It’s too late to buy a pallet of water from Costco.  @GovRonDeSantis has ordered the DOT to close the bridges.  The storm is here, and it’s already made landfall.

How do you take shelter?  Easy, the 4 things I mentioned above.  Okay, there’s probably a few more, but those are the big ones.

1) Steel is out of stock and all major structural orders are coming straight from the mill. This means you need a mill order.
2) Engineering teams are stretched thin already. You better lock down your team, ASAP.  People that make calls looking for an engineering company in June of 2027 will either go without or get a C or D level firm.
3) Order your long lead equipment like your life depends on it.  The same engineering and material availability constraints exist in the vendor’s supply chain too.  This takes rigorous project management.
4) Make direct relationships in industrial freight.  You need your imports to clear customs and you need your loads to get delivered on time. Not gonna be easy.

Later, we can talk more about the trades and factory software.  But those don’t even come into play if you can’t secure a project team with a predictable CAPEX budget and a schedule you can hit.  Now, layer in tariffs and shortages… see how hard this is?

With that dire warning, are we having fun yet?  I certainly am, 21 years of preparing for the big one, and the day has come. I have more than enough food and water on hand for me and my neighbors… and I’ve already waxed the surfboard.  No way I’m missing the waves 🏄‍♂️

Stay safe in the storm!

-your neighborhood engineer 

CC: @thereforgepod @ThaaatColin @ChangRobotics

posts.name: SMX 🇺🇸
posts.text:
Naval Ravikant once shared a story about Bill Gates shorting Tesla, a bet that could ultimately cost him more than $10 billion.

Gates had taken a massive short position against Tesla, reportedly equivalent to roughly 1% of the company’s total shares.

Naval suggested that if Tesla became the world’s most valuable company by a wide margin, the losses could be so enormous that even someone as wealthy as Bill Gates could face financial ruin.

But what fascinated Naval wasn't the money. It was Elon Musk’s reaction.

Musk was genuinely confused. How could someone who publicly championed clean energy financially bet against a company working to accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy?

The scale of US AI investment is unlike anything seen before.

Multiple roommates.  Ramen noodles.  Near public transportation.  Respect to the people who do whatever it takes.  

I worked as a bartender.  Bar-back. $2.15 an hr plus whatever tips got shared.  Worked at a retail store. Never had benefits at any job.  

Had 5 roommates in a 3 br apt.  Ate lousy food out of cans and ate  a ton of peanuts and shit food  at happy hour.  Had credit cards ripped up.  Etc.  

But I learned a ton.  Taught me what was right and wrong about running a business by watching my bosses and their bosses 

Yeah I know. It was much easier then, when inflation was 15 pct and national unemployment was 10 %.  I know I was fortunate when I finally got fired from the store, and had to start my own business with zero cash.   Bill collectors everywhere. 
Even luckier when I found my first customer so I could pay my bills

But I recognize it’s so much harder today.  

Which is why I respect the people who are willing to do what it takes to get started

One of the most useful things to measure after earnings isn't the size of the gap.

Measure how much of that gap survives.
A stock that gaps 12% and keeps 11% has processed the new information very differently from one that gaps 12% and finishes up 2%.

The announcement creates the gap.
The price action afterward tells you what traders ultimately decided about the move.
